title: Philosophy, Logic and Human Existence (GST 212)
description: General-studies course on the nature of philosophy, logic and reasoning, critical thinking, ethics and the meaning of human existence.

topics.title: What Is Philosophy?
topics.summary: Meaning, branches and method of philosophy, and African philosophy.

notes.b: Philosophy (Greek philo 'love' + sophia 'wisdom') is the rational, critical inquiry into fundamental questions about reality, knowledge, value and reasoning. Its main branches are metaphysics (the nature of reality and being), epistemology (the nature, sources and limits of knowledge), ethics or moral philosophy (right and wrong conduct), logic (the principles of correct reasoning), aesthetics (beauty and art) and political philosophy. Socrates' method of questioning (the Socratic method, or elenchus) exposes contradictions to reach clearer understanding; he held that 'the unexamined life is not worth living'.
k: Metaphysics: reality; epistemology: knowledge; ethics: conduct

notes.b: African philosophy examines questions from African experiences and worldviews. Currents identified by Henry Odera Oruka include ethnophilosophy (collective worldviews, e.g. Placide Tempels' Bantu Philosophy), philosophic sagacity (reflective thought of wise individuals), nationalist-ideological philosophy (e.g. Nyerere's Ujamaa, Nkrumah's consciencism) and professional philosophy. The Ubuntu idea — 'I am because we are' — emphasises communal personhood.
k: Oruka's four trends of African philosophy

topics.title: Logic: Arguments, Deduction and Induction
topics.summary: Propositions, arguments, validity and soundness, deductive and inductive reasoning.

notes.b: Logic studies the principles of correct reasoning. A proposition is a statement that is either true or false. An argument is a set of propositions in which some (premises) are offered as support for another (the conclusion). Words like 'therefore', 'hence' and 'thus' indicate conclusions; 'because', 'since' and 'for' indicate premises. Aristotle is regarded as the father of (formal) logic.

In a deductive argument, if the premises are true the conclusion must be true; a deductive argument is valid if its form guarantees this, and sound if it is valid and its premises are actually true. The classic categorical syllogism: 'All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal.' Inductive arguments move from particular observations to general conclusions that are probable, not certain (e.g. 'Every malaria patient we treated with ACT recovered; therefore ACT cures malaria'). Science relies heavily on induction.
k: Valid: true premises guarantee a true conclusion

topics.title: Informal Fallacies and Critical Thinking
topics.summary: Common fallacies of reasoning and habits of a critical thinker.

notes.b: A fallacy is an error in reasoning. Ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument. Appeal to authority (argumentum ad verecundiam) relies on an authority outside their field. Appeal to the people (ad populum) argues something is true because many believe it. Straw man misrepresents an opponent's view. Hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from too few cases. Post hoc ergo propter hoc assumes that because B followed A, A caused B. Begging the question (circular reasoning) assumes what it tries to prove. False dilemma presents only two options when more exist. Slippery slope claims one step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences.
k: False dilemma: only two choices offered

notes.b: Critical thinking is the disciplined evaluation of claims and arguments. It involves identifying assumptions, checking evidence and sources, considering alternative explanations, recognising bias and suspending judgement until the evidence is adequate. In health care it guards against misinformation and supports evidence-based practice — for example, questioning claims that a herbal product 'cures all diseases'.

topics.title: Epistemology: Sources and Limits of Knowledge
topics.summary: Rationalism, empiricism, scepticism and the definition of knowledge.

notes.b: Knowledge is traditionally defined as justified true belief (Plato). Rationalists (Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz) hold that reason is the primary source of knowledge; Descartes' methodical doubt led to 'Cogito, ergo sum' ('I think, therefore I am'). Empiricists (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) hold that knowledge comes from sense experience; Locke described the mind at birth as a tabula rasa (blank slate). Kant attempted to synthesise both: concepts without percepts are empty, percepts without concepts are blind.

Scepticism questions whether certain knowledge is possible; Hume doubted our knowledge of causation, saying we only observe constant conjunction. Other claimed sources of knowledge include testimony (authority), intuition, memory and revelation. The scientific method combines observation, hypothesis, experiment and revision, and Karl Popper argued that scientific theories must be falsifiable.
k: Testimony and memory are sources of belief

topics.title: Ethics and Human Existence
topics.summary: Ethical theories, the meaning of human existence, freedom and responsibility.

notes.b: Consequentialism judges actions by their outcomes; utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill) seeks the greatest happiness for the greatest number. Deontology (Kant) judges actions by duty and rules; Kant's categorical imperative says act only on maxims you could will as universal laws and treat persons always as ends, never merely as means. Virtue ethics (Aristotle) focuses on developing good character (courage, temperance, justice) aiming at eudaimonia (flourishing). Ethical relativism holds that morality varies between cultures.
k: Utilitarianism: greatest happiness for the greatest number

notes.b: Existentialism (Kierkegaard, Sartre, Camus) emphasises individual freedom, choice and responsibility; Sartre declared that 'existence precedes essence' — humans create their own meaning. The mind–body problem asks how mind relates to body: Descartes' dualism treats them as distinct substances; materialism holds that only matter exists. Questions of free will versus determinism bear on moral responsibility.
